title: The Forty-Eight Methods of Buddha-Recitation by Name
author: Zheng Wei'an
excerpt: Composed by the lay Buddhist Zheng Wei'an (published by the Buddhist Studies Bookshop, 1933)

inline.s: Composed by the lay Buddhist Zheng Wei'an
(published by the Buddhist Studies Bookshop, 1933)
Editor's note:
Master Hanshan said:

"Recite the Buddha's name thus and apply the mind thus: when you have recited to the very end of life and only a single sound of Amitābha Buddha appears before you, with a unified mind undistracted, you will naturally see Amitābha Buddha come in person to receive and guide you. In one thought you attain rebirth in the Pure Land, forever freed from birth and death, rising high to Ultimate Bliss, born by transformation in a lotus — such is the proof of a lifetime of Buddha-recitation."
(from the Dream Wanderings Collection
Instruction to the Assembly of Practitioners at Yihua)

This book teaches concretely and practically how to apply the mind and recite amid every circumstance. Read it often, pondering, comprehending, and practicing it, and you will surely be forever freed from birth and death and rise high to Ultimate Bliss.

blocks.text: Author's Preface

inline.s: As for the Pure Land, its Dharma gate is vast. The many people of superior goodness reborn there by following the Buddha's teaching flock from the ten directions, countless as raindrops. Some, though not devoted to recitation, nor to reciting the name within it, have still had their names inscribed on high and sit firm on the golden terrace — because they rode a great vow, or came by wondrous awakening, or had perfected many blessings, or upheld the power of the precepts, or excelled in visualization; so without skillful means the mind opened of itself. Today, visualization is not easily accomplished, the precepts are not easily kept in full, myriad blessings cannot be awaited overnight, wondrous awakening is not won by dull faculties, and a firm great vow is rarer still. If you do not rise above the rest by honest recitation of the name, you will sink long in the sea of suffering and endure rebirth without end; even the compassion of a thousand Buddhas will hardly save you. So this one practice gathers all three capacities and swiftly brings them home to the Pure Land. No skillful means excels it. Deep or shallow, in accord or apart, each chooses for himself. Strive on, and do not mislead yourself.

blocks.text: Guarding the Manas Faculty

inline.s: Since you recite with this mind, you need not dwell on mixed good or evil affairs. Even when daily life forces you to meet circumstances and handle unavoidable business, once done, let it go
(once handled, let it go)
, and do not let it cling and entangle, obstructing your mindfulness of the Buddha; and the reason your mindfulness entangles because the mind-ground works
(the sixth consciousness)
busying itself with affairs
(because it busies itself with affairs)
. When recitation brings the mind-ground to radiance, the mind-ground turns naturally wondrous in observation
(the sixth consciousness brings forth its wondrous function, observing the marks of all dharmas and the capacities of living beings — it becomes the wisdom of wondrous observation)
, and you should know that Buddha-recitation turns the ordinary into the noble; it is the foremost method of liberation, in the world and beyond.

[Mind-ground] Here "mind" means consciousness (the sixth consciousness): the seat governing the body, and the ground where all affairs arise; hence "ground." [Wisdom of Wondrous Observation] The wondrous observation of the marks of all dharmas and the capacities of living beings, wielding the function of expounding Dharma and cutting off doubt. [Manas faculty] 1. One of the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind); it means the seventh consciousness (manas). "Faculty" means that which generates. The objects of the first five faculties are form-dharmas of the four great elements (earth, water, fire, wind), giving rise to the first five consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body); the object of the manas faculty is mental dharma, giving rise to mind consciousness. 2. Also called mind-ground, meaning the sixth consciousness (mind consciousness).

blocks.text: Guarding Against Speech-Karma

inline.s: Since you recite with this mouth, do not let your tongue idly play with killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying. If such a thing comes up, reflect that one who recites the Buddha's name should not speak so, then recite several times with vigor to rouse yourself and wash it away.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name with an Upright Body

inline.s: [Upright body] Here "body" means conduct and bearing. To make the body upright is to rectify one's conduct and bearing.
Since you recite with this body, in all walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, keep it always upright
(your conduct and bearing must always be upright)
. If the body is upright
(if conduct and bearing are upright)
, the mind is at once pure; verify it yourself
(you can test it yourself)
, and truly it does not deceive me
(there is no deception at all)

blocks.text: Reciting the Name While Passing the Beads

inline.s: With each recitation, pass one bead through your fingers. Recite only the four syllables, not mingled with the six, for the four are easier to bring into one stream. Either pass the bead on the syllable "A" or on the syllable "Tuo"; fix your rule and let it not fall into confusion. This is one way of using beads to bind the mind.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name Aloud

inline.s: When spirit and wits grow dull, or idle thoughts rise in confusion, rouse your energy and recite aloud. After a few hundred recitations the whole state of mind changes. The ear faculty is the keenest and outer conditions enter easily; sound stirs the mind and random thoughts blaze up. Only reciting aloud guards the ear faculty and opens the mind's spirit: the mind hears its own voice, every sound brisk and full, and all idle talk of right and wrong is naturally dismissed.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name Softly

inline.s: When your spirit is scattered, or exhaustion presses hard, there is no need to recite aloud: gather your spirit in and recite softly and finely. When breath is full and steady and energy revives, you may recite aloud.

blocks.text: Diamond Recitation of the Name

inline.s: If mind and breath are out of harmony, or place and company make it awkward, and neither loud nor soft recitation suits, then move only the lips in the diamond recitation. However many or few, every syllable must pass through the mind.

blocks.text: Silent Recitation of the Name

inline.s: Or again, when neither loud nor soft recitation suits, passing beads seems trifling, and the diamond recitation still leaves traces, there is an ancient and most ingenious skillful means: no need to move the mouth, no sound need be uttered. Simply fasten the mind on one object, and gently with the tongue faculty
(the tongue is one of the six faculties, hence "tongue faculty"; here it means the tongue)

tap against the front teeth. The mind's recitation follows, the sound distinct. The sound does not pass its aperture; the nature of hearing melts inward; mind seals the tongue's mechanism, which draws forth the faculty of mindfulness. Entering the stream through hearing, one turns hearing back to the self-nature. These three merge, and thought after thought is penetrating; in time it becomes the contemplation of mind-only consciousness.

[Faculty of mindfulness] One of the five faculties: to be mindful only of the right path and its aids, to contemplate single-mindedly, letting no falsehood enter. [Five faculties] Faith, effort, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom. These five dharmas are the root from which the noble path is born; hence "five faculties."

blocks.text: Reciting the Name While Regulating the Breath

inline.s: Or when breath is calm and mind at peace, first visualize your body in a circle of light, quietly watching the tip of your nose and attending to the breath. With each breath, silently recite Amitābha Buddha once. As a skillful means for regulating the breath, be neither slow nor hurried; mind and breath lean on each other, following the breath in and out. Walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, you may practice anywhere. Let it not be interrupted; keep it always as your secret practice. When the mind is gathered long, breath and thought are both forgotten and body and mind become equal to space. Recite until utterly proficient: the mind's eye opens and samādhi suddenly appears — this is the Pure Land of mind-only.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name According to Capacity

inline.s: When dullness is heavy, recite while walking; when distraction is heavy, recite while sitting upright. If neither suits you, then kneeling, standing, or lying down for a while, use whatever skillful means you can and recite according to capacity to save yourself. The point is never to let a single thought of the four-syllable great name be forgotten; this is the chief art for subduing the demon of the mind.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name Everywhere

inline.s: Whether in clean places or filthy, in leisure or in haste, in high spirits or in disappointment, simply turn the light back and reflect: these states I have passed through hundreds of thousands of millions of times since distant kalpas past; only in the one matter of recitation and rebirth have I failed to settle the account, and so I turn and turn again in rebirth without ever getting free. Now I will harbor no other thought
(from now on I harbor no other thought)
, but only vow that this mind of recitation shall not break off this thought even unto death
(I simply vow that this mind of recitation shall not break off this thought even unto death)
. Why? Once the thought of recitation is broken, mixed thoughts — good, evil, and neutral — arise again.

Even when answering the calls of nature, or when a woman is in labor, just keep reciting: the greater the suffering the more you recite, the sharper the pain the more you recite. It is like a child crying for its mother, never minding whether she is annoyed. If the child feared annoying her and did not call, then a little one fallen into a latrine pit would have only death, and when would it ever see its mother again?
[Neutral]
Neither good nor evil, and not to be marked or distinguished.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name with or without a Fixed Rule

inline.s: What is fixed is this: at morning and evening set a regular course, and from now until death neither add nor take away. In the remaining hours, recite one phrase if you can, whether aloud or softly. The ancients said: "Speak one sentence less, recite the Buddha's name one time more." How true
(so it is)
! How true!

[Speak one sentence less, recite the Buddha's name one time more] Certain Directions to the West says: "Speak one sentence less, recite the Buddha's name one time more; beat the thought to death, and your Dharma-body is allowed to live."

blocks.text: Reciting the Name Before an Image and Apart from Images

inline.s: When facing an image, take it as the true Buddha, confined to no direction, asking not which of the three bodies
(not whether Dharma-body, reward-body, or response-body)
, but simply think: I rest in the one mind
(I rest in the one mind)
, the mind rests in the one Buddha
(the mind rests in the one Buddha)
, facing him with gratitude and mindfulness
(facing the true Buddha with gratitude and longing)

, and your sincerity may be known. When sincerity and reverence reach their height, response is surely granted. If there is no image, sit upright facing west, and when a thought arises, think of Amitābha Buddha's light abiding above your crown; then phrase by phrase nothing falls empty, and dark karma dissolves.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in the Midst of Busyness

inline.s: One phrase if you can manage one, ten if you can manage ten. So long as amid a hundred busy tasks you find a moment's leisure, you may set down body and mind and recite clearly. Bai Letian's poem says: "Walking, Amitābha; sitting, Amitābha; though busy
(even if)
as an arrow, never apart from Amitābha." Here the intent of the ancients may be seen.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Leisure

inline.s: All the suffering people in the world cannot find leisure, and so cannot practice. Now you have leisure! And you have heard this method of recitation. You must make it close-woven and continuous, rousing and gathering yourself, only thus not wasting your time. If you recite carelessly and idly it will not serve; you will waste the months and years, betray the four kindnesses, and when impermanence suddenly arrives one day, with what will you answer it?
[Four kindnesses]
The kindness of parents, of living beings, of the country, and of the Three Jewels.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in High Station

inline.s: The blessings of this life come from cultivation in past lives. Those of noble and honored station
(people of distinguished birth and eminence)
are mostly the rebirths of ascetic monks of high attainment
(are mostly the rebirths of ascetic monks of high attainment)

. Yet glory and splendor cannot last, and if you create more evil you will surely sink. Reflect: rather than carry your karma away, better to sail your boat with the current. Establish a hall for recitation, or support monks who recite, or print Pure Land books, or commission images of Amitābha. Cry out from the high ground, and half the effort brings double the result. Still more should you resolve firmly on rebirth and be a model of practice for all, rich and poor alike
(a model of practice for all, noble and humble alike)
, an envoy of the Dharma King
(become an envoy of the Buddha)
. How honored and surpassing is that?

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Low Station

inline.s: Alas! To be a servant in another's employ is suffering indeed! Not to seek liberation is suffering upon suffering! Know that the four-syllable Buddha-name makes no distinction of noble or base, high or low, old or young, man or woman. If only each day at dawn you face west with all your heart, call the name ten times, and seek birth in Ultimate Bliss without break, you will gain benefit in this life, and at the end of life
(when you leave this world)
you will surely attain rebirth. Amitābha Buddha is truly the life-saving ship in the sea of suffering.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Quiet Subtlety

inline.s: [Reciting the name in quiet subtlety] There may be an error of transcription or typesetting; it should probably read "reciting the name in quiet reflection." [Reciting the name in quiet reflection] Silently settle the single thought "Amitābha Buddha" in your mind, and a hundred poisons cannot invade you.
Since you have wisdom, do not let it run into madness
(do not fall into wild wisdom)
; it is best to recite quietly and subtly
(in quiet reflection)

to make it firm. Know that when the wise recite, those who recite in the world multiply; when the wise recite, those who practice in outer paths easily turn back. Why? Because the renown of wisdom awakens them, and the working of wisdom saves them.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name Honestly

inline.s: To seek neither fame nor profit, to show off no talents, and to practice honestly — this is the rarest of all. The patriarchs said: "In Chan practice you cannot find a single dull-witted person." The reciters of today suffer precisely from not being dull-witted. The words "honest and simple" are a straight highway to birth in the West. Why? Because the honest person adds not a hair's-breadth of idle thought beyond the four syllables of Amitābha Buddha.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Joyous Celebration

inline.s: Whether you rejoice over a person or celebrate an event, even a small occasion is a happy state in human life. Know that this joy is illusory and cannot last. While the good time is here, turn the light around and recite; then relying on the Buddha's light, amid favorable conditions you will shed many evil thoughts, auspiciousness will come unbroken, your practice will go as you wish, and on to the end of life you will be reborn in Ultimate Bliss. Is that not a great joy?

blocks.text: Reciting the Name with Vows

inline.s: Reciting the name is fundamentally for rebirth, yet the Buddhas' majestic light is inconceivable: when you call their names, your wishes accord with your mind. Hence the scriptures say recitation brings ten kinds of benefit
(see the appendix:
"A Brief Explanation of the Ten Supreme Merits Gained in This Life through Buddha-Recitation"

Rather than pray to ghosts and spirits, mix in ritual repentance, make broad vows of evil import, or trust sorcerers on the side, it is better to place your hopes in recitation. Someone may ask: "What if there is no response?" The answer: "Before you have even recited, you already worry about no response. That very cause of no response must bring the fruit of no response. Such a cause, such a fruit — how fearful!"

blocks.text: Reciting the Name for Deliverance

inline.s: [Reciting the name for deliverance] In adverse circumstances, one recites the name and is thereby freed and released.

Whenever adverse circumstances confront you, they are deluded conditions meeting you face to face. Do not give rise to further evil thoughts and bring on future evil fruit. Simply follow along: what can be avoided, avoid; what can be dissolved, dissolve. Go along with causes and conditions, and do not forget to recite. The Buddha has immeasurable wisdom; when his merit, virtue, and light are bestowed, circumstances turn at once — of this there is no doubt.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Shame and Zeal

inline.s: Whatever evil fruit has ripened from this life or past lives, its bitter retribution must come. Therefore all suffering is all evil. You must not blame ill fortune; you should only feel shame that your practice came so late. Whenever you think of the Buddha, the hairs of your body stand on end and your inward organs
(the five viscera)

seem to split, and you are moved to grief and ardor, so pained you scarcely wish to live. In this way each word flows from your very marrow, and only then is it the true realm of recitation. Nowadays monks and laypeople either recite with the mouth while the mind races, or gather the mind while reciting but let it go dim the moment they stop. Others interject idle chatter mid-recitation. Thus even if they recite to the end of their days they will have no spiritual response. Those who see them say recitation and rebirth are ultimately empty words — but is that the Buddha's fault?

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Earnest Entreaty

inline.s: To be in a situation where nothing can be done and feel no grief is not human. Yet to be in such a situation and only grieve — is that to understand the Buddha-nature? Since you grieve, you should think of escaping suffering; you should think of bringing all living beings to ultimate escape from suffering; you should think that the Buddha is called greatly compassionate because he can pull living beings out of suffering. I recite with a grieving heart, seeking the Buddha's compassion to pull me from my suffering — how earnest should that recitation be
(how earnest that recitation should be)

blocks.text: Reciting the Name as Offering

inline.s: [Reciting the name as offering] Calling the name and reciting the Buddha is an offering of Dharma. The offering of Dharma made with the mind surpasses every offering of wealth.

On festivals or the Buddha's birthday you may offer incense, flowers, lamps, and fruit as the season allows; this is an offering of wealth, not of Dharma. The offering of Dharma made with the mind surpasses every offering of wealth. In recent times heretical teachings have flourished, and their way of offering gathers a great array of sacrificial goods — what good does that do for practice? Such sects as "Pure Universal Salvation, Imperial Ultimate, Longevity Prime" and "Wuwei Mahayana" invite the planchette, practice circle-light divination, summon souls and draw in ghosts, drain families of their wealth, and deceive the world with wild words. As for the one gate of recitation, it is utterly different
(the gate of recitation is an offering of Dharma, utterly different from the offerings of wealth made by those sects)
. Those with discernment must never be deluded by them
(those with discernment must never be deluded by those heretical sects)

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Repayment

inline.s: The kindness of parents is the greatest of all. How should it be repaid? To provide food and drink, to win merit and fame — by worldly standards such repayment is not bad, yet in the end it settles nothing. I repay only by reciting and dedicating the merit to them for the West: this already plants a diamond seed, and when they emerge again they will have their hour of liberation — how much more, then, can boundless karmic obstacles be wholly dissolved? Whoever wishes to repay kindness must know this method.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name as Giving

inline.s: Whenever you see someone in distress, first give them bodily comfort, then open and guide their mind, urging them to recite. As it is said: to relieve suffering for a time, giving is most urgent; to relieve suffering through kalpas, recitation is essential. If you see someone in danger and lack power to save them, at once recite for them, to settle their spirit. Or recite aloud in the still of night, as an offering to ghosts and spirits. In years of great war or plague, recite in the fifth watch, and you can dispel vengeful spirits. Reflect that this one sound of Amitābha Buddha of mine reaches upward to the highest heaven
(up to the very summit of the world)
, and downward to the very bottom of the wind-wheel
(down to the very bottom of the world)
, and living beings in dust-mote lands beyond number benefit at that moment; such giving is inconceivable.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name with Mind Recollecting and Mind Hearing

inline.s: The mind recollects, then the tongue moves; the tongue moves, and it returns to the mind. Since the tongue makes a sound, the ear hears it of itself — this is mind recollecting, mind hearing. When mind recollects and mind hears, the eyes cannot look astray, the nose cannot smell astray, the body cannot move astray; the one master within is invited out by the four syllables of Amitābha Buddha.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name within the Sound

inline.s: Once the sound of recitation is utterly proficient, among the six sense-objects only sound remains. The whole function of the six faculties rests in the ear: the body no longer feels itself circling, the tongue no longer feels itself moving, the mind no longer feels itself discriminating, the nose no longer feels itself breathing, the eyes no longer feel themselves closed. The two perfect penetrations of Guanyin and Dashizhi are then one
(at this stage, the ear-faculty penetration of Avalokiteshvara and the recitation penetration of Mahasthamaprapta are one)

. Nothing is not penetrating; nothing is not perfect. Faculty is sense-object, sense-object is faculty, faculty and sense-object are consciousness: the eighteen realms melt into one. At first you may not be attuned; in time you will enter of yourself.

Whenever you recite, choose a clean plot four or five feet square, walk one circuit clockwise, then begin to utter the sound slowly, gradually raising the pitch. When you have recited three circuits in this way, you will feel your mind's sound shine forth, circling through space, wrapping the ten directions, pervading the whole Dharma-realm — this is to settle body, mind, and world within the sound of recitation. That is, with body and mind settled in the sound, you recite the Buddha's name. This is a supreme state, able to extinguish the defilements of the mind; practice it diligently.
[Eighteen realms]

The six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind), the six sense-objects (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, mental objects), and the six consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness) together are called the "eighteen realms."

blocks.text: Reciting the Name within the Light

inline.s: Sound is the sound of the mind; light is likewise the light of the mind. Where the mind's sound circles, there the mind's light shines forth. To dwell in the mind's sound and recite is to dwell in the light and recite. This too is a supreme state, able to extinguish the defilements of the mind; practice it diligently.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name within the Mirror

inline.s: The mind's sound circles, the mind's light shines forth, and the essence of mind discloses itself. This one true mind is like a great perfect mirror, penetrating without obstruction: the ten directions and three times, my Buddha and living beings, the bitter wheel of the turbid world, the lotus calyxes of the Pure Land — all are reflections in the mirror. Within the sound is within the light; within the light is within the mirror. This is the most supreme state, able to extinguish forever the defilements of the mind; apply yourself diligently to it.

blocks.text: Uninterrupted Recitation of the Name

inline.s: Recite in the morning, recite in the evening, recite when there is nothing to do, recite when there is much to do, recite in clean places, recite in filthy places, until no thought is not the Buddha. Even if daily dealings sometimes interrupt you, the words break off but the true lifeline cannot. When your practice reaches this point, a continuous stream comes easily.

blocks.text: Unmixed Recitation of the Name

inline.s: To be unmixed is precisely calm abiding. Calm abiding is the working of concentration. When mixed thoughts cease, right mindfulness appears. Mixed thoughts are of three kinds: good, evil, and neutral. Only when these three are wholly removed is one unmixed. The mind must be still and quiet; being still, good and evil thoughts do not arise. The mind must be alert and awake; being alert, neutral thoughts do not arise. Beyond the Buddha there is no thought, so one is always still; within the thought there is the Buddha, so one is always alert.

blocks.text: Non-abiding Recitation of the Name

inline.s: Not abiding is precisely contemplation. Contemplation is the working of wisdom. The previous phrase is past, the next is yet to come, and the present phrase likewise does not abide. Perfectly clear, yet unobtainable; unobtainable, yet perfectly clear.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name as Chan and Buddha Both

inline.s: To look into a huatou is called Chan inquiry; to sit or to still the thoughts is called sitting Chan. Inquiry and sitting are both Chan. Chan and Buddha are both mind. Chan is the Chan of the Buddha, the Buddha is the Buddha of Chan — how does the gate of recitation hinder Chan inquiry or sitting Chan? Moreover, one who inquires into Chan can take these four syllables, Amitābha Buddha, as a huatou, reciting them over and over without letting go; though he does not speak of Chan inquiry, Chan is right there within it. One who sits in Chan must reach the point where a single thought resonates and all is suddenly as if held in emptiness. When recitation reaches the state of a unified mind undistracted, is that not resonance? When it reaches the point where the mind is empty, is that not everlasting resonance? In the very act of reciting, neither dull nor scattered, calm abiding and contemplation, concentration and wisdom, are perfected in every thought. If you would seek Chan elsewhere, where then could that Chan be?

blocks.text: Reciting the Name as Precepts and Buddha Both

inline.s: Keeping the Buddha's precepts governs the body; holding the Buddha's name governs the mind. Hold them long and the mind becomes pure; hold them long and the mind becomes empty. The nature of mindfulness and the nature of precepts are not two. To keep the precepts rigidly brings no liberation; to recite rigidly, then at the approach of death you will smash through the gate of ghosts and leap out of the three realms. If you already have skill in the precepts, dedicate that to the West and you will surely be born in the middle grade. If you cannot attend to both, then simply recite diligently, as though your hair were on fire.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name as Doctrine and Buddha Both

inline.s: The whole canon of scriptures arises from the mind; if the mind holds no Buddha, doctrine is in vain
(studying the doctrine is studying in vain)
. Yet whose mind lacks the Buddha
(yet whose mind lacks the Buddha?)
? It is only that one does not recite
(it is simply that one does not recite oneself)
! Among the schools of doctrine there is none who does not read the Surangama Sutra; and of those who read it, none does not slight Mahasthamaprapta and prize Guanyin

(of those who read the Surangama Sutra, none does not slight the chapter on Mahasthamaprapta's perfect penetration through recitation and prize the chapter on Avalokiteshvara's perfect penetration through the ear faculty)
. This single view alone
(this single view alone)

has already become the root of birth and death. Even if you learn every kind of knowledge and skill, it only waters the sprout of suffering, and at the juncture of birth and death it is of no avail. I urge you to let go at once and be reborn in the West to behold Amitābha in person. If you cannot let go, then dedicate to the West the merit of studying and expounding the scriptures, and make the four great vows; even that is not wasted
(it does not fall empty either)

. If you spread the one gate of the Pure Land and explain in detail the merits of recitation, then every lift of the eyes and every stirring of thought adorns the Western Pure Land, and what doubt remains of birth in the highest grade?
[Four great vows]

Living beings are boundless; I vow to save them all. Afflictions are endless; I vow to cut them all off. Dharma gates are measureless; I vow to learn them all. The Buddha's path is unsurpassed; I vow to accomplish it.

blocks.text: Reciting Without Reciting

inline.s: A task is barely finished, a sentence barely done, and before you have even set about reciting, the four-syllable Buddha-name comes rolling out — a sign that samādhi will easily be attained.

blocks.text: Reciting Yet Not Reciting

inline.s: Recite without slackening, brisk and full and ever more brisk and full. As you recite, you clearly hold these four syllables and your thought does not turn, yet the four syllables suddenly pause: there is no thought that is the four syllables, nor any thought apart from them, nor any thought beyond them. This is called a supreme state briefly attained; it is not the true emptiness of mind.

Yet if you recite diligently and this state appears again and again, the mind will gradually become empty. If, because of one thought of emptiness, you drift into dullness, that is called being without wisdom. Know that the emptier the mind, the more alive the recitation; the emptier the mind, the purer the recitation. With the self within the Buddha's mind, reciting the Buddha within my mind — where then are emptiness and non-emptiness? It is like the sun and moon, radiant, riding their jeweled palaces, circling Mount Sumeru, streaming around and illumining the whole world. Ah! What wondrous enlightenment and perfect radiance is this!

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Solitude

inline.s: When a monk cultivates the path he does not seek companions; for recitation, solitary stillness is best. High or low as suits you, slow or quick as capacity allows, forging it all into one piece — this is precisely the time. Know that the body may be alone but the mind is not. The minds of all Buddhas and of Amitābha have never for a moment abandoned me; when a thought arises the Buddha knows it, when I open my mouth the Buddha hears it — why worry about solitude?

If the gate of the Pure Land is not yet clear to you, buy more Pure Land books and read them — such works as the Amitābha Sutra, the Contemplation Sutra, Master Zhizhe's Ten Doubts, Chan Master Tianru Ze's Pure Land Questions and Answers, Chan Master Dayou's Guide to the Pure Land, Longshu's Pure Land Essays, The Pure Land Morning Bell, The Western Public Evidence, Certain Directions to the West, Yunqi's Collected Works, and the Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra. Read them diligently. Here I have named only the plain and easy ones; beyond these there are far too many to list. Or seek out those who understand the Pure Land and question them.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in a Set Period

inline.s: To set a period is to set seven days as the term. If you set the period alone, you may take dried provisions, fruit, ginger, and sesame oil, four kinds, as food, and incense for the burner, lamp oil, a sitting cushion, a chair, a padded coat, a wind hood, a chamber pot, and coarse paper, eight kinds, as supplies. Apart from these twelve
(apart from these twelve)

, keep nothing else, and you can spend the seven days without dealings with others, reciting freely. If five or six people resolve together to set a period, you must invite a master to guard the seven days, establish strict rules and bind yourselves to them beforehand; the guarding master sees to all your rising and resting, food and drink, incense, flowers, lamps, and fruit, and then those sharing the seven days can also recite with all their hearts. If one is bound by emotional views and does not know what helps or harms practice, this should not be done carelessly.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Assembly

inline.s: When four or five people happen to gather and form a recitation meeting, first agree on the rules before opening your mouths. Recite only the four syllables, one syllable to one strike of the wooden fish
(one syllable to one wooden fish)
, and use a small hand-bell to strike particularly on the syllables A and Tuo. Do not let it fall into unevenness, which only scatters the mind.

blocks.text: Helping Others Accomplish Recitation of the Name

inline.s: Whether you settle someone in a quiet place, or join with them in setting a period of recitation, or tell them of the Pure Land, or lend them Pure Land books, or break through their doubts about recitation, or firm up their resolve to recite — of all merits, this is the supreme one.

If at someone's death you recite for them, or have the sick person hold the four syllables Amitābha Buddha in mind, recollecting and reciting as they can, so that they see the Tathagata and pass away to rebirth, you have brought their Dharma-body and wisdom-life to accomplishment.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Calamity

inline.s: Whenever in calamity someone resolves to recite, there is sure to be a wondrous response. Though spears fill the land and plague ravages a whole district, whoever seeks the Buddha's protection — one person, one is safe; a hundred, a hundred are safe. It is not that the Buddha plays favorites; it is response without intent within the equal light. Why? When a thought stirs and a sound is voiced, and you feel Amitābha Buddha's light abiding above your crown, then every thought is complete, every thought firm, every thought enduring; graced by the Buddha's light and guarded by auspicious spirits, you will surely escape the calamity. Do not let your thought turn aside.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Dreams

inline.s: When your vow is firm and your practice mature, and what is close-woven by day is so by night, then you will naturally recite in dreams — a sign of rebirth. Harmonize and press on diligently, neither retreating nor growing wild.

blocks.text: Reciting the Name in Illness

inline.s: Illness is the threshold of death. Death is the gate between ordinary and noble, pure and defiled. In illness you should contemplate death, diligently recite, and resolutely await death; then there will surely be light to receive and guide you, fulfilling your vow of rebirth. But if in illness you pause for even a moment's thought, then all your attachments, terrors, afflictions, and schemes, every kind of mixed thought, appear at once — and at the juncture of birth and death, how will that serve? Long ago a monk fell gravely ill and cried "Ayo!" Aware that this was wrong, he recited Amitābha Buddha. He hurt so much he could not stop himself, so it was one cry of "Ayo," one recitation of Amitābha Buddha, day and night without cease. When he recovered he told people: "In my illness I recited 'Ayo' and 'Amitābha Buddha.' Now that I am well, Amitābha Buddha is still here, but where the two words 'Ayo' have gone I do not know!" Excellent! This is one who pressed on diligently in illness.

blocks.text: Holding the Name at the Moment of Death

inline.s: Only keep the four characters Amitābha Buddha in mind and never forget them. If you are able to recite aloud, recite aloud; if you can only recite softly, recite softly. And if you can do neither, then hold the four characters silently in your heart and let them never be lost. Those who attend you at the bedside should likewise constantly remind you of these four characters. Know that all the stray paths you have wandered through a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives are cut off cleanly in this very moment, by a single thought. Why is this so? The wheel of the six realms is governed by one thought as master. If that thought is fixed entirely upon the Buddha, then though the body decays, the spirit does not scatter, and following that single thought one is reborn in the Pure Land. Alas! Only keep the four characters Amitābha Buddha in mind, and never forget them.

blocks.text: Making Vows, Confessing, and Reciting the Name

inline.s: Alas! How many people in this world fail to understand the recitation of the Buddha's name! The Confucians cast Buddhism aside as heterodox and refuse to recite; monastics make of the recitation a set routine and do not know why they recite; those of wild wisdom know there is a Buddha yet disdain to recite; the foolish and deluded do not know the Buddha and so are unable to recite. This is the general picture
(speaking broadly)

, and even among village men and women, who upon hearing of cause and effect do come to know the recitation and practice it, they yet hanker after blessings in a life to come and so remain seeds of the wheel of rebirth. Of those who seek one that recites in order to transcend birth and death, there are barely one or two in a hundred. Know that once a person recites the Buddha's name, he should take up the Buddha's compassionate heart, practice the Buddha's compassionate deeds, make vast vows, and deliver sentient beings; for all defilements and karmic entanglements he should universally repent; and every merit, great and small, he should dedicate toward the Western Land. Only this is the true cause of reciting the Buddha's name.

blocks.text: Appendix: A Plain Explanation of the Ten Transcendent Benefits of Reciting the Buddha's Name in This Present Life

inline.s: Explained by the Venerable Elder Master Changzhen

A single recitation of the Buddha's name is the crystallization of ten thousand kinds of merit, possessing an inconceivable, mighty spiritual power. It is the compassionate ferry across the sea of birth and death, the bright lamp in the endless night. Especially for the sentient beings of the Latter Age of the Dharma, whose faculties are inferior and who face many conditions for backsliding. As the Great Jewel Heap Sutra says: "In the Latter Age, among untold millions upon millions who cultivate, scarce one attains the Way (realizes the fruit of the path); only by relying on the recitation of the Buddha's name are they able to transcend birth and death." The modern eminent monk Master Daoyuan likewise said: "For the sentient beings of the Latter Age, there is no way to end birth and death save by reciting the Buddha's name, and no way to deliver sentient beings save by reciting the Buddha's name." (Master Daoyuan: Lectures on the Amitābha Sutra.) This shows that the practice of reciting the Buddha's name is the sovereign remedy for the sentient beings of the Latter Age.

Some people suppose that the practice of reciting the Buddha's name is meant for the elderly — a way of idling away their days and awaiting death, useful only at the last hour. These are all one-sided and mistaken views. In truth, our own mind is the Buddha; to recite the Buddha's name is to recite the mind — this is what is meant by "the mind is what makes the Buddha." "Cast the Buddha's name into a confused mind, and the confused mind cannot but become the Buddha (the Buddha-mind)." Layman Xia Lianju put it well: "Recite Amitābha, recite on straight ahead — it turns out that it is Amitābha reciting Amitābha." From this it is clear that a single name-recitation can release one from birth and death, escape the wheel of rebirth, be reborn in the Pure Land, and perfectly realize bodhi — truly the shortest cut within the shortest cut. One further point must be made clear: recitation does not only bring great benefit at the moment of death; it brings great benefit even in this present life. Master Yinguang said: all things can be accomplished by reciting the Buddha's name to seek their fulfillment — except doing evil.

The ten kinds of transcendent benefit gained in this present life through reciting the Buddha's name, as set forth in this article, form a fairly comprehensive summing up. These were all spoken personally by the Buddha and were excerpted from the Buddhist scriptures. The Buddha never speaks falsely — do not doubt them in the least! For the convenience of beginners, I have made this humble and plain explanation. If there is anything inappropriate, I respectfully beg your correction.
1. One constantly enjoys the invisible protection of all heavenly gods.

All the heavenly gods within the celestial realms revere the Buddha Dharma. The merit of our recitation is certain to move the gods, who rejoice, praise it, and protect us in unseen ways. Therefore, the person who recites, without praying for the dispelling of calamities and the averting of misfortune, naturally has calamities dispelled and misfortune averted; without praying for his family's peace, his family is naturally at peace. For the reciter this is but a small benefit gained in this present life. For the gods, too, it is the accumulation of merit, so that both sides are benefited.
2. One constantly enjoys the ever-present protection and following of all bodhisattvas.

The task of the bodhisattvas is, above, to seek the Buddha Way, and, below, to transform sentient beings. For this reason they constantly manifest immeasurable bodies, roaming the ten directions to deliver those who are bound by conditions. The sentient beings who recite the Buddha's name are bound by conditions to the buddhas and bodhisattvas; when beings in the sea of birth and death single-mindedly call out the name, they are sending a cry for help to the buddhas and bodhisattvas. Hence the ancient worthy said: "In the sea of birth and death, to recite the Buddha's name comes first." Calling the name for rescue is the cause; the bodhisattva, hearing the sound and saving from suffering, is the condition. When cause and condition meet and the spiritual response is joined, then misfortune turns to fortune and suffering gives way to joy — this is the fruit. Through the ages many bound sentient beings, having called on the name amid disasters and distress, have turned peril into safety through that calling; and having gained the benefits of recitation, they have given rise to faith and made vows, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma. "First entice them with what they desire, then lead them into the Buddha's wisdom" — this is the skillful means by which the bodhisattvas transform and deliver sentient beings.
3. One constantly enjoys the day-and-night protection and remembrance of all buddhas, and Amitābha Buddha constantly radiates light to gather in and receive this person.

Constantly protected and remembered by all buddhas: to protect means to guard; to remember means to bear in mind. The Amitābha Sutra says: "These good men and good women are all protected and kept in mind by all the buddhas, and every one of them attains non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-sambodhi (the unexcelled, perfect enlightenment)." This shows that the person who recites the Buddha's name is protected and kept in mind by all the buddhas. Because the power of the buddhas' protection and remembrance is inconceivable, the mind of their cultivation can never retrogress, until they attain the Buddha's wisdom — anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. According to this, even if in this life one cannot be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, still, having already planted the roots of goodness, one will never retrogress, and there will surely come a day when one is reborn in the Pure Land, sees the Buddha, and hears the Dharma.

Amitābha Buddha radiates light to gather in and receive: Amitābha Buddha is also called the Buddha of Boundless Light. The Buddha's light of wisdom pervades the ten directions, transcending space. The Buddha's radiance is a thousand million times greater than the light of the sun; the sun's light is cut off by a single wall. The Buddha's radiance shines on all things, and nothing whatsoever can block it. "Amitābha" means Boundless Light and Boundless Life, and is the Dharmakāya of the Buddha — that is to say, the Buddha-nature inherent in every person. For the reciter, karmic hindrances are dissolved and body and mind become pure; when the mind is pure, the mind is the Buddha. This is the principle of "when falsehood departs, the true is revealed."
4. The person who recites the Buddha's name is illumined all about his body to a distance of forty li; no evil ghosts can harm him, and no snakes, dragons, or poisons can affect him at all.

The everlasting true mind with which every person is endowed is like a great round mirror that mirrors heaven and earth, possessing boundless light. But veiled by the dust of many lives, it grows dim and colorless. A single recitation of the Buddha's name is a purifying agent that dispels false thoughts; when false thoughts are dispelled, the mind's radiance is revealed, and the body emits a light that reaches forty li away. This is real and not false. The Collected Works of Master Ouyi records: In Tongcheng County, Anhui, there were two men, Jia and Yi, who went out to trade; in time Jia fell ill and died in a foreign land. Yi buried him and brought back his belongings, giving them to Jia's wife. As her husband was young and strong, she wondered how he could have died so suddenly, and suspected Yi of murdering him for his wealth. Yi felt deeply wronged, yet had no way to prove his innocence. He went to Jia's grave and wept, pouring out his grievance. Suddenly Jia's voice came close to his ear, saying: "You have been kind to me, and my wife has wronged you. I can cling to your body and return home to explain it to her clearly." So Yi turned back. Along the way Jia conversed with him, just as in life, though only the voice was heard — no form was seen. Once, Yi stumbled by accident and nearly fell. Without thinking, he recited, "Amitābha Buddha!" At that, Jia said in an alarmed voice from afar: "Why do you cast a light and frighten me?" Hearing that recitation emits light, Yi recited the Buddha's name several times more. Then Jia's voice moved still farther away, saying: "When you recite the Buddha's name, your chest radiates a dazzling light, and I cannot come near you. Please go back and tell my wife to come to the grave, and I will explain it to her clearly." Yi did as he was told. Through this, Yi came to feel deeply the inconceivable power of the Buddha, so he gave up commerce, left home to become a monk, and cultivated with undivided devotion. In time he became a great monk.
Again, in the year

, Layman Yang Changping of Chengdu, passing East Gate Bridge one day, stepped on a stone and nearly fell, and without realizing it uttered the recitation "Amitābha Buddha!" That night he had a dream in which five gaily adorned, beautiful women invited him to walk with them. His heart was moved, and he went along with them to a certain street and number; they went in and beckoned to him. At that moment an old man with a white beard blocked his way, saying: "You are a reciter of the Buddha's name — do not go in." He nonetheless pressed on with all his might, and then suddenly awoke. Finding the dream strange, Yang went in person the next day to that street and number and asked the master of the house about the scene of the night before. The host said: "No five beautiful women came. Only, last night my family's mother dog gave birth to
puppies, of which

were female spotted dogs, and one male dog died the moment it was born." Hearing this, Yang broke out in a cold sweat. He thought: had he not uttered a single recitation, he would have gone off and become a dog. From then on he served the Buddha all the more devoutly and often cited this matter to admonish others. The above was personally heard from Yang by Layman Fan Longyi (now
years old, residing at the Recitation and Care Home of Bao Guo Temple in Lezhi).

All demons and spirits fear the light and fear the Buddha's name. The Universal Gateway Chapter says: Suppose in the three thousand great thousand lands there are yakṣas and rākṣasas everywhere, wishing to harm people. When they hear a person call upon the name of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, those evil ghosts dare not even look at him, much less do him harm. Nor will any evil dragons, venomous snakes, or savage beasts harm him. "If savage beasts surround you, with fearful fangs and claws, by the power of thinking on Avalokiteshvara they hasten at once to the boundless regions (fleeing swiftly far away)." "Poisonous serpents and vipers and scorpions, in their venom blazing like smoke and fire, by the power of thinking on Avalokiteshvara, hearing the sound, turn back of their own accord (draw away)." As for poisons, there is also clear instruction: "Curses and all manner of poisons, meant to harm the body, by the power of thinking on Avalokiteshvara, fall back upon the one who sent them (harm-doing harms oneself)." All of the above was spoken personally by the Buddha. Though it speaks of calling upon Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, reciting the Buddha's name is just the same.
5. One is not subject to flood, fire, enemies and thieves, swords and arrows, imprisonment, or death by sudden calamity or wrongful persecution.

The sentient beings of the five turbid ages are beset by all manner of calamities and afflictions without end. Here are listed flood, fire, enmity, bandits, guns and cannon (in ancient times swords and arrows — in our day guns and cannon, all of them weapons that kill; the calamity of sword and arrow also embraces the havoc of war), imprisonment, and death by sudden disaster or wrongful oppression, or a wrongful fall into the evil destinies. In truth, the disasters are far more than these; they are cited merely as representative examples.

The three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion are the root of all evil and the source of every calamity. The person who recites the Buddha's name, in thought after thought, clears away the three poisons and dispels afflictions; without praying for the removal of calamity, he is naturally freed from calamity in the unseen. If in ordinary times he single-mindedly calls on the Buddha's name, then at the critical moment the Amitābha of his own nature will of himself rescue the Amitābha within the minds of sentient beings, and carry him through misfortune to good fortune. If one does not recite in ordinary times, then when disaster befalls, the heart is filled with terror and panic, the faculties are in a whirl, and it is difficult to recall the Buddha's name. Moreover, the secret of reciting the Buddha's name is utmost sincerity and reverence. Master Yinguang said: "With one portion of reverence, one portion of karmic offense is dissolved and one portion of blessing and wisdom is increased; with ten portions of reverence, ten portions of karmic offense are dissolved and ten portions of blessing and wisdom are increased." In this we must hold fast!
6. Karmic actions committed in the past are all wiped away. The wronged lives one has killed are released and delivered, and no longer hold them in thrall.

Since beginningless kalpas we have created karmic evil that is measureless and boundless. If karmic offense had shape and volume, the whole of space could not contain it. Therefore we suffer through long kalpas and are unable to escape. Master Miaokong's Forty-eight Methods of Holding the Name says: "To save one from a moment of suffering, giving is most urgent; to save one from the suffering of ten thousand kalpas, reciting the Buddha's name is most essential." The sutra says, "With a single sincere recitation of the Buddha's name, one can wipe away the heavy sins of birth and death committed over eighty million kalpas." For the wronged lives we have killed in the past, we should earnestly and sincerely call on the Buddha's name to resolve the enmity and untie the knot, so that they may receive the Buddha's compassionate aid and be reborn in a fortunate destiny. Then naturally enmity turns to grace, misfortune to blessing, and the evil retribution of seeking revenge dissolves without a trace.
7. One's dreams by night are upright, or one dreams of the sublime and wondrous bodily form of Amitābha Buddha.

Dreams are manifestations of the mind alone. Those heavy in desire have many lewd and defiled dreams; those heavy in anger have many terrifying dreams. The person who recites the Buddha's name is pure in body and mind, sleeps peacefully at night, and will not have evil or depraved dreams. Moreover, once in bed, silently holding the Buddha's name or quietly listening to a recording of the recitation can nourish the mind and settle the spirit, both counteracting insomnia and dispelling evil dreams. If in a dream one encounters a frightful sight or a nightmare, a single recitation of the Buddha's name instantly turns it into nothing.

Recite the Buddha's name honestly and practice with fine, unbroken effort; false thoughts gradually dissolve, and the mind's radiance gradually appears. When the minds of sentient beings are pure, they see the Buddha; the Buddha at all times and in all places manifests his presence (words of Master Jingkong). When the water is clear, the moon appears of itself — and then one can behold the sublime and majestic wondrous form of Amitābha Buddha. But one must not on that account give rise to a mind of joy or attachment. Far from being beneficial, it will bring harm. Master Yinguang said: "Of late, among those who cultivate, there are many cases of falling under demonic influence. These all come from a restless, reckless mind, eagerly hoping for a spiritual response and for splendid states to appear. You should understand: need it be said that the states which appear are the work of demons? Even a sublime and wondrous state, if a single thought of greedy attachment and delight arises in it, will bring obstacles and harm."
8. One's heart is ever joyful, one's complexion is lustrous and radiant, one's strength is vigorous, and all one does is auspicious.

For the sentient beings of the Saha world, the body is the root of suffering. A lifetime is mostly spent in terror, resentment, sorrow, and pain. Only the person who recites the Buddha's name, with a pure mind, recites single-mindedly, dissolving karma as conditions arise, and is not turned by circumstances. His heart is filled with the joy of Dharma; his countenance is full and radiant, and disease naturally disappears. Health and long life come without being sought — and these are but by-products of the recitation. For the person who recites, all buddhas rejoice, dragons and gods protect, good conditions grow, and whatever he does is necessarily auspicious. Master Jingkong said that in Taiwan there was a male layman, over ninety years of age, who every day walked thirty thousand steps and recited the Buddha's name thirty thousand times; his body was healthy, his spirit full, and his back and spine straight. When the time of his death comes, he will surely be free of all the suffering of illness and pass on in peace.
9. One is ever revered, beloved, and honored by all the people of the world.

The person who recites the Buddha's name is inwardly pure, meets others with harmony, broadly forms good conditions, and finds joy in helping others. Confucius said: "He who respects others is ever respected by them; he who loves others is ever loved by them." (He who respects others plants a good cause, and being ever respected by them reaps a good fruit; he who loves others plants a good cause, and being ever loved by them reaps a good fruit.) Planting such a cause, reaping such a fruit, to be revered, beloved, and honored by people is a matter of necessity.

The nine articles above are all great benefits gained in this present life through reciting the Buddha's name. That view which holds the recitation to be a means of idling away one's days awaiting death, and of use only at the last hour, collapses of itself without needing to be refuted.

10. At the moment of death, one's heart is without fear, right mindfulness is present, and one sees Amitābha Buddha together with the host of sages, who hold a golden lotus to guide and welcome one to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the West.

Death is the most sorrowful matter in life, and it is one no one can escape. At the moment of death, an emperor of supreme power, a magnate of countless wealth, and a beggar who owns nothing at all are exactly the same. The power and riches in their hands are of no help whatsoever. Only the person who recites the Buddha's name is able at that time to be without attachment and without fear, single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land. At the same time, he will surely receive the Buddha's guidance to be reborn in the land of the lotus. From then on he transcends the ordinary and enters the holy, until he attains Buddhahood. Of Amitābha Buddha's forty-eight great vows, the nineteenth is the vow of hearing the name and awakening the aspiration, and the twentieth is the vow of receiving and guiding one at the moment of death. The vow reads: "When I attain Buddhahood, may the sentient beings of the ten directions, on hearing my name, awaken the bodhi mind, cultivate all kinds of merit, practice the six pāramitās, firm and never retreating; and, dedicating their roots of goodness, vow to be born in my land, single-mindedly mindful of me day and night without ceasing. At the end of their lives, I, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, shall appear before them. In the space of a moment (in the twinkling of an eye), they shall be born in my Buddha-land (territory) as avivartika (non-retreating) bodhisattvas. Should this vow not be fulfilled, may I not attain perfect enlightenment (if this vow cannot be realized, I vow never to become a Buddha)." This is Amitābha Buddha's guarantee to the sentient beings who recite his name. Is there still any room for doubt?

The ten kinds of benefit above are fully recorded in the scriptures and were proclaimed from the Buddha's golden mouth. Since they bring benefit both in this present life and in the life to come, then of all the essential Dharma-gates within the world and beyond it, there is none more important than reciting the Buddha's name. Only be diligent — do not doubt!

The ten great benefits set forth in this article are all recorded in the Buddhist scriptures and were spoken personally by Śākyamuni Buddha. Since they benefit both the present life and the life to come, then whether viewed from the standpoint of worldly Dharma or of the transcendental Dharma, among all Dharma-gates there is none more important than the practice of reciting the Buddha's name.

But the practice of reciting the Buddha's name is a Dharma-gate that is "easy to practice and hard to believe." Many who study Buddhism do not wholly understand it, and some perhaps still doubt it. As Master Lianchi of the Ming dynasty said in his essay "On Not Being Single-Minded in Recitation" in the Bamboo Window Miscellany: "Formerly, when I was studying at a certain temple, one day the abbot said to the assembly that on the Ghost Festival we should hold a Yulanpen assembly. I supposed we would surely set out a meal and offer it to the community, yet in the end no offering was set out — the abbot merely led the assembly in reciting the Buddha's name for three days. Again, when the head of a certain temple was taken into custody by the authorities, the abbot of the temple gathered the community to perform a Buddhist rite in prayer for his rescue. The assembly thought they would chant sutras and hold mantras, but in the end they only recited the Buddha's name aloud. Both of these matters lay beyond the expectations of ordinary reasoning. One may see that the thoughts and deeds of the great worthies are not commonplace and are well worth learning from. Yet many who recite the Buddha's name today, though they profess single-minded cultivation of the Pure Land, still, in order to prolong their years, chant the Medicine Buddha Sutra; in order to dissolve karmic offenses, bow in the Emperor Liang Repentance; in order to rescue themselves from calamity, recite the disaster-dispelling mantra; in order to seek wisdom, recite the Avalokiteshvara text. They set aside the Buddha-name they ordinarily recite, deeming the recitation of no avail. Why not consider this: Amitābha Buddha is the Buddha of Boundless Life, and those born in his land have life immeasurable as well — how much the more may one beseech a life of a hundred years in the human world? The Contemplation Sutra on the Buddha of Immeasurable Life says, "With a single sincere recitation of the Buddha's name, one can wipe away the heavy sins of birth and death committed over eighty million kalpas." How much the more can the calamities before one's very eyes be dispelled? The Larger Sutra of Immeasurable Life says, "I with the light of wisdom broadly illuminate the boundless realms." For the person who recites, Amitābha constantly illumines his body with the light of wisdom — why worry about lacking wisdom? "A single recitation of the Buddha's name is the agada medicine, holding in check all the ten thousand diseases. If you do not believe it and will not take it, of what use is it?" This important instruction, read today, still carries guidance of very pertinent significance.

We who recite the Buddha's name must believe deeply in the Buddha's words. "If the Buddha's words cannot be believed, what words can be believed?" Only be diligent in reciting the Buddha's name, and never doubt in the least! Doubt of itself creates obstacles, and then it will be very hard indeed to obtain the benefits of the recitation.
